worksheet.title: Send a Message
worksheet.subtitle: One script can start another with a message
worksheet.learning_goal: I can read a broadcast message that starts another script.

parts.title: Broadcast and receive
parts.text: A script can send a message to other scripts. This is called a broadcast. Bit's last block is 'broadcast go'. Pixel's script starts with 'when I receive go'. So Bit runs first, sends the message 'go', and THAT message starts Pixel. Pixel waits until it hears 'go'.

parts.title: Bit goes first
parts.prompt: The green flag starts Bit from home 0: forward 2. What number does Bit land on? Then Bit sends the message 'go'.

parts.title: Pixel hears the message
parts.prompt: When Pixel receives 'go', it runs from home 5: back 2. What number does Pixel land on?

parts.title: What starts Pixel?
parts.prompt: Pixel has no green-flag block. What makes Pixel's script start? Write it. Would Pixel move if Bit never sent the message? Circle YES or NO.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: A broadcast is a message one script sends. A 'when I receive' script waits for that message and starts when it arrives. So Bit's broadcast 'go' is the EVENT that starts Pixel — no message, no start.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Grade 2 · Events & Parallel Scripts
teacher_guide.title: Send a Message
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students meet sending and getting a message: Bit can send a message ("go"), and Pixel starts only when it gets that message ("when I receive go"). The message is itself an event. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer needed — paper and a pencil. You read the prompts aloud. Optional: two counters on a number line 0 to 5 (green Bit, purple Pixel), and a card that says "go" you can hand over to act out sending a message.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Bit runs, then sends "go"; Pixel was waiting for "go" and starts only then.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — Bit lands on 2 and sends "go"; Exercise 2 — Pixel gets "go" and lands on 3.
3. Let them try. Students name what starts Pixel, and say what happens if "go" is never sent (Ex 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 2 — Pixel gets "go" and runs: 5, back 2 → 3.
Exercise 3 — Pixel is started by the message ("when I receive go"). If Bit never sent "go", Pixel would not move — it stays home at 5.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: thinking the green flag starts Pixel. It is the message that starts Pixel.
Make it easier: hand a "go" card to the child running Pixel to act out the message.
Make it harder: ask why Pixel runs after Bit, not at the same time (the message is sent at the end of Bit's moves).

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
In plain terms: students write and run instructions that are started by an event, like clicking the green flag or getting a message.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, change what starts them or one move, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child sees that Pixel runs only because Bit sent the message, and finds both landings.
